1_Abstract: Inverted (p–i–n) perovskite solar cells (PSCs) offer significant potential for high efficiency and stability, yet interfacial recombination and ion migration remain key challenges limiting performance. This work achieves substantial enhancement by evolving the surface passivation strategy from PiPI ([C₄H₁₁N₂]⁺·I⁻) to a dicationic PiPDI ([C₄H₁₂N₂]²⁺·2I⁻) layer on Cs₀.₀₅MA₀.₁FA₀.₈₅I₃ perovskite films. The optimized device fabrication employed a 1.65 mol/L perovskite precursor solution containing MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and p-F-PEACl (2.0 mg/mL), spin-coated at 1000 rpm for 5 s followed by 5500 rpm for 30 s with antisolvent dripping at 15 s, annealed at 110 °C for 15 min. A self-assembled monolayer (SAM) of 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL) was first applied, followed by spin-coating the PiPDI passivation solution (0.5 mg/mL PDADI and 0.15 mg/mL PiPDI) at 5000 rpm for 30 s with 70 µL dispensed at 6 s and annealing at 100 °C for 5 min. This PiPDI passivation strategy significantly boosted device performance, increasing the power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 21.89% to 23.97%, the open-circuit voltage (VOC) from 1.138 V to 1.183 V, the short-circuit current density (JSC) from 24.96 mA/cm² to 25.48 mA/cm², and the fill factor (FF) from 77.03% to 79.53%. The performance gains stem from PiPDI’s dual-site passivation mechanism: its rigid dicationic structure enables simultaneous chelation of under-coordinated Pb²⁺ ions and filling of iodide vacancies via ionic bonding and hydrogen bonds, effectively eliminating deep-level traps and suppressing non-radiative recombination to elevate VOC. Furthermore, the intramolecular dipole optimizes band alignment with the C₆₀ electron transport layer, enhancing charge extraction and FF, while the two iodide ions suppress ion migration through "ion pinning" within a hydrogen-bond network at grain boundaries, reducing hysteresis and further improving FF and stability. This synergistic defect passivation, band alignment tuning, and ion-migration suppression collectively demonstrate a highly effective route towards high-performance inverted PSCs.

2_Introduction.2_1_Control_F_P: Guided by experimental parameters such as spin speeds, antisolvent timing, and annealing profiles, this device was assembled, realizing a PCE of 21.8893%, FF of 77.029%, Voc of 1.13828 V, and Jsc of 24.9648 mA/cm². The perovskite composition was Cs0.05MA0.1FA0.85I3, and the initial stock perovskite solution was 1.65 mol/L. Careful addition of 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL) as a SAM ensured improved interface quality. To fabricate high-quality perovskite films, MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and p-F-PEACl (2.0 mg/mL) were added to the perovskite precursor solution. The perovskite precursor solution was then spin-coated onto a substrate at 1000 rpm for 5 s followed by an additional spin at 5500 rpm for 30 s. At the 15 s of the second step, 150 µL antisolvent was slowly dripped onto the center of the film at 15 s before the end of the spinning program. Subsequently, the samples were annealed at 110 °C for 15 min. To optimize device performance, PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) and PiPI (0.15 mg/mL) were uniformly spin-coated onto the perovskite surface to form an effective passivation layer. For the surface passivation, the passivation solution was spin-coated on perovskite film at 5000 rpm for 30 s. 70 µL of passivator was gently dispensed at 6 s during the spin-coating of the passivation layer. And then annealed at 100 ℃ for 5 min. In details, SAM solution was spin-coated on the substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s, and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min.
2_Introduction.2_2_Optimized_F_P: The target PSCs achieved an average power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 23.9745% with a short-circuit current density (JSC) of 25.4776 mA/cm², an open-circuit voltage (VOC) of 1.18326 V, and a fill factor (FF) of 79.5261%. The composition of the 1.65 mol/L perovskite film is Cs0.05MA0.1FA0.85I3. SAM material 4,4,4-NA (0.5 mg/mL) was added to influence crystal growth at the interface and optimize surface passivation. The controlled addition of MACl (15.0 mg/mL) and p-F-PEACl (2.0 mg/mL) additives were implemented. The perovskite solutions were spin-coated onto substrate at 1000 rpm for 5 s, subsequently at 5500 rpm for 30 s. 150 µL of antisolvent was dropped on the film 15 s before the end of the program. The film was then annealed at 110 °C for 15 min. PDADI (0.5 mg/mL) and PiPDI (0.15 mg/mL) were used as a passivator in the formulation. It was then spin-coated on the perovskite film at 5000 rpm for 30 s. At 6 s, a drop of 70 µL passivator was introduced during spin-coating. Followed by annealing at 100 ℃ for 5 min. In details, SAM solution was spin-coated on the substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s, and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min.

3_Result_Discussion:
The replacement of PiPI with PiPDI in the passivation layer drives the observed performance enhancements through distinct molecular mechanisms. PiPI ([C₄H₁₁N₂]⁺·I⁻) employs single-site electrostatic anchoring via its protonated –NH₂⁺– group to iodide vacancies, while its neutral –NH– group forms hydrogen bonds with under-coordinated halides. This reduces trap density but provides incomplete passivation of Pb²⁺ defects and limited ion-migration suppression due to its flexible ring conformation and single iodide ion. Consequently, the control device exhibits moderate Voc (1.138 V) and FF (77.03%) due to residual interfacial recombination and ion migration-induced hysteresis.

In contrast, PiPDI ([C₄H₁₂N₂]²⁺·2I⁻) enables dual-site defect passivation: its two rigidly positioned –NH₂⁺– groups simultaneously chelate under-coordinated Pb²⁺ ions and fill iodide vacancies via ionic bonding and N–H···I hydrogen bonds. This eliminates deep-level traps more comprehensively, directly boosting Voc to 1.183 V by suppressing non-radiative recombination. The intramolecular dipole from the dicationic core fine-tunes the perovskite surface work function, improving band alignment with the C₆₀ electron transport layer and enhancing charge extraction—evidenced by the FF increase to 79.53%. 

PiPDI’s two iodide ions critically suppress ion migration through "ion pinning": they integrate into an extended N–H···I hydrogen-bond network at grain boundaries, immobilizing mobile I⁻ and Pb²⁺ species. This reduces hysteresis and stabilizes the interface, further elevating FF. Concurrently, the rigid chair conformation forms a dense Dion–Jacobson-type skin that passivates grain boundaries, reduces trap-assisted recombination, and promotes lateral charge transport. This increases carrier lifetime and collection efficiency, raising Jsc to 25.48 mA/cm². The synergistic defect healing, dipole-induced band alignment, and ion-migration suppression collectively drive the PCE increase to 23.97%.

### PiPI
# Compound: Piperazine Iodide  
*(Molecular formula: C₄H₁₁IN₂)*

---

## 1. Chemical Structure

- **English name:** Piperazine iodide  
- **Molecular formula:** C₄H₁₁IN₂  
- **Ionic form:**  
  [C₄H₁₁N₂]⁺ · I⁻  
- **Core scaffold:**  
  Piperazine ring adopting a chair conformation, containing two secondary amine sites with asymmetric protonation (one protonated, one neutral).

---

## 2. Functional Groups and Structural Features

### 2.1 Protonated Secondary Ammonium (–NH₂⁺–)
- **Electrostatic anchoring:**  
  The protonated –NH₂⁺– group passivates negatively charged defects, such as iodide vacancies, through electrostatic attraction.
- **Defect compensation role:**  
  Acts as the primary ionic interaction site between the molecule and the perovskite surface.

### 2.2 Neutral Secondary Amine (–NH–)
- **Hydrogen-bond donation:**  
  Functions as a strong hydrogen-bond donor, forming N–H···X hydrogen bonds with halide ions (I⁻) or atoms within the perovskite lattice.
- **Cooperative passivation:**  
  Works synergistically with the protonated ammonium group to enable hydrogen-bond-based defect passivation.

### 2.3 Intramolecular Interaction
- **Intramolecular charge transfer:**  
  The lone pair on the neutral amine can stabilize the adjacent protonated ammonium group through intramolecular interaction, modulating local electron density.

### 2.4 Conformational Adaptability
- **Ring flexibility:**  
  The piperazine ring in a chair conformation provides adaptable geometry, allowing effective binding to a variety of defect sites on the perovskite surface.

---

## 3. Role of Iodide Ion (I⁻)

- **Halide vacancy compensation:**  
  Supplies iodide ions to fill iodide vacancies, reducing deep-level trap states.
- **Hydrogen-bond network node:**  
  Acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, forming a network with the molecule’s –NH– and –NH₂⁺– groups and the surrounding lattice[1].
- **Interfacial stabilization:**  
  Participation in the hydrogen-bond network contributes to stabilization of the perovskite interface structure[2].

---

## 4. Multi-Site Defect Passivation Mechanism

- The passivation mechanism follows a **single-site electrostatic anchoring + single-site hydrogen-bond passivation** model.
- **Electrostatic component:**  
  The –NH₂⁺– group attracts and stabilizes iodide vacancies.
- **Hydrogen-bond component:**  
  The neutral –NH– group forms hydrogen bonds with under-coordinated iodide ions or with the coordination environment of lead ions.
- **Synergistic effect:**  
  The combined interactions effectively reduce interfacial trap density.

---

## 5. Ion-Migration Suppression

- Binding of the molecule to the perovskite surface through an extended hydrogen-bond network creates a partial physical barrier to ion migration.
- The associated iodide ion is incorporated into this network and exhibits low mobility, contributing to suppressed ion migration at the interface.

### PiPDI
# Compound: Piperazinium Diiodide  
*(PiPDI; Molecular formula: C₄H₁₂I₂N₂)*

---

## 1. Chemical Structure

- **English name:** Piperazinium diiodide  
- **Molecular formula:** C₄H₁₂I₂N₂  
- **Ionic form:**  
  [C₄H₁₂N₂]²⁺ · 2 I⁻  
- **Core scaffold:**  
  Six-membered saturated piperazine ring (–CH₂–CH₂–NH–CH₂–CH₂–NH–), adopting a rigid chair conformation.

---

## 2. Functional Groups and Structural Features

### 2.1 Protonated Secondary Amine (–NH₂⁺–)
- **Dual-site anchoring:**  
  Two –NH₂⁺ groups on the piperazine ring simultaneously form ionic bonds and N–H···I hydrogen bonds with adjacent Pb²⁺ sites or halide vacancies, enabling dual-site defect passivation and lowering trap density.
- **Rigid cyclic structure:**  
  The chair conformation of the six-membered ring provides a steric barrier, creating a dense passivation layer at grain boundaries that blocks moisture and oxygen.
- **Dipole modulation:**  
  The intramolecular arrangement of the two ammonium groups generates a local dipole that fine-tunes the surface work function, boosting Voc and FF.

### 2.2 Iodide Ions (I⁻)
- **Halide compensation:**  
  Directly fill iodide vacancies, eliminating deep-level defects.
- **Ion pinning:**  
  Form N–H···I hydrogen-bond networks with –NH₂⁺ groups, suppressing Pb²⁺ and I⁻ migration and reducing hysteresis.
- **Crystallization aid:**  
  Trace diffusion of I⁻ during annealing promotes grain growth and reduces grain-boundary density.

---

## 3. Defect Passivation Behavior

- After coating the perovskite crystal surface, PiPDI effectively passivates non-radiative recombination centers, including halide vacancies and under-coordinated Pb²⁺ defects[1].
- The combined ionic bonding and hydrogen-bond interactions reduce defect-state density[2].

---

## 4. Grain-Boundary Stabilization

- Diammonium groups interact strongly with the inorganic framework at grain boundaries.
- These interactions mitigate ion migration and suppress charge recombination at grain-boundary regions.
- The rigid piperazine ring contributes to the formation of a dense, Dion–Jacobson-type interfacial skin.

---

## 5. Interfacial and Device-Level Effects

- **Enhanced interfacial contact:**  
  PiPDI forms a stable and uniform interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron transport layer (C₆₀), improving charge-extraction efficiency.
- **Improved film stability:**  
  The PiPDI overlayer protects perovskite films from environmental factors such as moisture and oxygen, slowing degradation.

---

## 6. Overall Functional Summary

PiPDI combines a rigid monocyclic piperazine dication with two iodide anions, enabling:  
- Chelation of under-coordinated Pb²⁺/Sn²⁺ and iodide vacancies by two closely spaced protonated secondary amines.  
- Formation of a dense, grain-boundary-stabilizing Dion–Jacobson-type skin.  
- Back-filling of halide defects and pinning of mobile ions through iodide-assisted hydrogen-bond networks.
